headline: Canada Start-Up Visa 2026: Requirements and the Pause
metaDescription: Canada's Start-Up Visa 2026: paused 30 June 2026, no new applications accepted. Support letter, CLB 5, settlement funds — and alternatives explained.

sections.content:
The Start-Up Visa Program is closed to new applicants. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) set intake to zero effective 1 January 2026, and no new commitment certificates from designated organizations have been accepted since 31 December 2025.

A transitional window allowed founders holding a valid 2025 commitment certificate to submit their permanent residence application until 30 June 2026. That deadline has now passed and was not extended, so the federal Start-up Business Class no longer accepts any new applications. Applications filed before the deadline are still being processed.
sections.title: The 2026 pause: no new applications

sections.content:
To qualify, an entrepreneur needed four things. First, a qualifying business: each applicant, up to five founders per application, had to hold at least 10 percent of the voting rights in the corporation. Second, a letter of support from a designated organization, which also sent a commitment certificate directly to IRCC.

Third, language proficiency of at least Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 5 in all four abilities — speaking, reading, writing, and listening — in English or French, from an approved test taken within the previous two years. Fourth, proof of settlement funds under IRCC's published table, separate from any business investment.
sections.title: The four requirements as they stood

sections.content:
Only organizations on IRCC's designated lists could support an application. A designated venture capital fund had to agree to invest a minimum of CAD $200,000 in the business, while a designated angel investor group had to agree to invest a minimum of CAD $75,000.

A designated business incubator worked differently: it had to accept the startup into its program, with no minimum investment required, though founders typically paid a program fee for mentoring, office space, and business development services. IRCC also capped the number of permanent residence applications it would accept at 10 startups per designated organization per calendar year.
sections.title: Designated organizations and investment minimums

sections.content:
Applicants had to show enough unencumbered, readily transferable money to support themselves and their family after landing, and the government would not support them financially. For a single applicant the published requirement was CAD $15,263, rising to about CAD $19,001 for two people, CAD $23,360 for three, and CAD $28,362 for four.

Since 30 April 2026, the processing fee has been CAD $990 plus a CAD $600 right of permanent residence fee for a spouse or partner, and CAD $270 per dependent child. Founders should confirm the current figures on canada.ca before relying on them, because IRCC updates the settlement-funds table annually.
sections.title: Settlement funds and fees

sections.content:
With intake at zero, founders should not pay any organization for a new letter of support, because it cannot lead to an application under the current rules. IRCC has signalled a replacement entrepreneur stream in its 2026-27 departmental plan, but no eligibility criteria or program parameters have been published.

In the meantime, founders considering Canada can look at provincial entrepreneur streams, the Self-Employed Persons Program where it fits, or a work permit route such as the Global Talent Stream or an intra-company transfer. Anyone holding a commitment certificate from 2025 should check the IRCC page directly for the latest status of their file.
